primary_meaning: In mainstream Christian interpretation, 'synagogue of Satan' (Revelation 2:9; 3:9) refers to a religious assembly that claims to be the true people of God ('those who say they are Jews and are not') but in fact opposes God and persecutes His faithful, thereby serving Satan rather than God. In the historical setting of Revelation, this is most commonly understood as the local Jewish communities in Smyrna and Philadelphia who denounced or slandered Christians to Roman authorities; theologically, the phrase asserts that the true 'Jew' / true Israel is defined by faithfulness to God in Christ, so those persecuting the church have forfeited the title. The related phrase 'assembly of the wicked' (Psalm 22:16; cf. Psalm 26:5) denotes the gathered company of evildoers surrounding the righteous sufferer, read christologically by Christians as the mob surrounding Christ at the crucifixion. In broader devotional and homiletical use, both phrases have come to symbolize any counterfeit or apostate religious body—a congregation outwardly religious but inwardly hostile to God.
primary_basis: Revelation 2:9 — 'the blasphemy of those who say they are Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan'
Revelation 3:9 — 'those of the synagogue of Satan, who say they are Jews and are not, but lie'
Psalm 22:16 — 'the assembly of the wicked have enclosed me' (read christologically via the crucifixion narratives)
Psalm 26:5 — 'I have hated the congregation of evildoers'
Romans 2:28–29 — true Jewishness is inward, of the heart (used to explain 'say they are Jews and are not')
Romans 9:6 — 'not all who are descended from Israel are Israel'
John 8:44 — 'you are of your father the devil' (parallel polemic against religious opponents of Jesus)
Revelation 12:9–10 — Satan as 'accuser of the brethren' (linking slander/accusation of Christians to Satan)

alternatives.meaning: Historical-literal reading: actual first-century Jewish synagogues in Smyrna and Philadelphia whose members informed on or slandered Christians, exposing them to Roman persecution; the polemic is intra-religious rivalry over who constitutes true Israel, not a statement about Jews in general.
basis: Revelation 2:9–10 (slander followed by imprisonment and tribulation)
Martyrdom of Polycarp and other early sources on Jewish-Christian conflict in Smyrna (extra-biblical support commonly cited in commentaries)

alternatives.meaning: The people in question are not ethnic Jews at all but Gentiles or Judaizing Christians falsely claiming Jewish identity or Jewish legal privileges (e.g., to avoid persecution or to impose law-keeping); on this view the text criticizes false claimants to Judaism rather than Jewish communities.
basis: Revelation 2:9; 3:9 ('say they are Jews and are not' taken at face value)
Galatians and Acts 15 background on Judaizers (argued by a minority of scholars)

alternatives.meaning: Typological/ecclesial reading: a symbol of any apostate or counterfeit church in any era—an institution claiming to be God's people while persecuting true believers. In classic Protestant historicist interpretation this was applied to the papacy/Roman Catholic Church; in Seventh-day Adventist and some other traditions it is applied to fallen or false Christianity generally.
basis: Revelation 17 (Babylon as false religious system) used as a parallel
2 Timothy 3:5 ('a form of godliness, denying its power')

alternatives.meaning: Supersessionist reading extended to Judaism as such: the phrase taken as a verdict that post-Christian Judaism collectively constitutes a Satanic assembly. Held in strands of patristic and later polemic; largely repudiated in modern mainstream scholarship and church teaching.
basis: John 8:44 (as used in patristic anti-Jewish polemic, e.g., John Chrysostom)

alternatives.meaning: Conspiratorial/racial readings (e.g., claims that modern Jews are impostor 'Khazars' and the 'synagogue of Satan' names them) found in fringe and antisemitic literature; rejected by biblical scholarship.

For 'assembly of the wicked' specifically: a non-christological reading as simply the psalmist David's own historical enemies encircling him, without messianic typology (standard in Jewish interpretation and in some historical-critical Christian scholarship).
basis: Psalm 22 read in its own historical setting

notes: The two phrases come from different corpora: 'assembly/congregation of the wicked' is from the Psalms (esp. Psalm 22:16), while 'synagogue of Satan' is unique to Revelation 2:9 and 3:9; Christian teaching often merges them into a single symbol of a false or hostile religious assembly. There is broad consensus on the general symbolic force—an assembly claiming divine legitimacy while actually opposing God and persecuting the faithful—but genuine scholarly debate persists over the precise referent in Revelation (actual Jewish communities vs. false claimants to Jewish identity) and over how far the phrase may legitimately be generalized. Modern commentators uniformly caution that the verse has a long history of antisemitic misuse and that its original context is an inner-Jewish/sectarian dispute over identity, not a blanket statement about Jews.
